title: Do-re-mi began as a medieval monk’s memory trick
body: In the early 11th century, the Italian monk Guido of Arezzo taught singers a hymn to John the Baptist, Ut queant laxis, in which each line starts one note higher than the last. The first syllables of those lines, ut, re, mi, fa, sol and la, became names for the notes, helping choirs learn chants much faster. Guido also helped develop the staff of lines for writing pitch, the ancestor of modern notation.

slides.heading: Oldest first
items: Guido names ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la
Sarah Glover turns si into ti
slides.explanation: Guido taught the syllables in the early 11th century, do replaced ut in the 1600s, and the English teacher Sarah Glover changed si to ti in the 19th century.

slides.heading: Ut became do
slides.text: In the 1600s, Italians swapped the closed syllable ut for the easier-to-sing do, a change often credited to Giovanni Battista Doni. French sometimes still uses ut.

slides.heading: Where ti comes from
slides.text: A seventh syllable, si, came from the initials of Sancte Iohannes in the hymn’s last line. In the 19th century, English teacher Sarah Glover changed it to ti.

slides.heading: Notes on your fingers
slides.text: Medieval teachers mapped notes onto the joints of the hand so singers could point to pitches. This ‘Guidonian hand’ bears Guido’s name, but its familiar form came later.
